dīghāvuupāsakasutta: [Dīghāvuupāsaka+sutta]  CL=7 The discourse preached by the Lord Buddha to the Sangha concerns a lay disciple, Dīghāvu, who was seriously ill. He had firm faith in (1) The Buddha, (2) The Dhamma, and (3) The Sangha. Dīghāvu observed the five precepts preferred by the arahants. He was endowed with the four characteristics of a sotāpanna and was progressing in the practice toward becoming an anāgāmi. The six characteristics associated with an anāgāmi that he cultivated are: (1) Meditating repeatedly on the impermanence of volitional formations (saṅkhāra). (2) Perceiving the unsatisfactoriness (dukkha) inherent in volitional formations. (3) Recognizing that the volitional formations, being unsatisfactory, are not self (anattā). (4) Resolving to abandon attachment to volitional formations. (5) Developing detachment from volitional formations  (6) Cultivating the perception of cessation regarding volitional formations. These six qualities are the Vijjābhāgiya Dhammas (factors of insight) and are included in the Maggañāṇa (knowledge of the path). With these six qualities, he became an anāgāmi and, after passing away, he was reborn in the Brahma realm (a higher celestial plane).

dīghāyukabuddha: [Dīghāyuka+buddha]  CL=8 Long-lived Buddha, Buddha with a long lifespan. When these Buddhas enter parinibbāna, their bodily relics remain as a single solid mass, like a large gold ingot, and only one stupa is built and venerated. During the time of these Buddhas, every 6 years or every 6 months, the Buddha himself recites the Ovāda Pātimokkha (exhortation) in the Sangha assembly, and only the Sangha Uposatha is observed. Other Uposathas are not performed. Until the disappearance of the sāsana (Buddhist dispensation), this Pātimokkha is recited. Moreover, only the direct disciples can perform the acts of giving novice ordination, higher ordination, and conferring dependence (nissaya). Other individuals are not allowed to perform these acts (Suttanipāta Commentary, 1, 193).
dīghāyukakamma:
[Dīghāyuka+kamma]  CL=8 Meritorious deeds that lead to longevity, good kamma that promotes long life. This kamma refers to the wholesome action of abstaining from taking the lives of others. It includes observing moral precepts, maintaining the five precepts, performing acts of generosity, engaging in healing practices, and consistently showing respect and reverence to those who are senior in age, monastic status, virtue, or experience.
Among these, the wholesome kamma of abstaining from taking life, while it may not directly result in rebirth in celestial realms, supports longevity in the following ways for those born in the human realm due to other kamma:
1. It destroys various dangers and threats.
2. It promotes the growth of wealth and prosperity.
These benefits in the course of one"s life (pavatti) contribute to and support a long lifespan.
